concepts.name: Population-level health thinking
concepts.summary: Explain that epidemiology studies patterns of disease in groups rather than diagnosing or treating individuals.

concepts.name: Person, place, time
concepts.summary: Recall that disease distribution is described by who is affected, where, and when.

concepts.name: Incidence and prevalence
concepts.summary: Distinguish new cases arising over time from all existing cases at a point or period.

concepts.name: Risk factors and exposures
concepts.summary: Identify exposures and outcomes and explain that a risk factor raises the probability of disease without guaranteeing it.

concepts.name: Epidemic, endemic, pandemic
concepts.summary: Recall the definitions of endemic, outbreak, epidemic and pandemic by comparison with expected frequency and spread.

concepts.name: Association versus causation
concepts.summary: Explain that an observed link between exposure and disease does not by itself show that the exposure causes it.

misconceptions.text: Prevalence and incidence mean the same thing.
If two things occur together, one must cause the other.
Epidemiology is only about infectious disease outbreaks.

concepts.name: Rates, risks and proportions
concepts.summary: Calculate incidence proportion, incidence rate with person-time, and point prevalence from data.

concepts.name: Relative risk and odds ratio
concepts.summary: Compute and interpret risk ratio and odds ratio from a 2x2 table.

concepts.name: Risk difference and attributable risk
concepts.summary: Calculate risk difference and attributable fraction and interpret the absolute impact of an exposure.

concepts.name: Cohort and case-control designs
concepts.summary: Describe how cohort and case-control studies select participants and which measures each can estimate.

concepts.name: Cross-sectional studies
concepts.summary: Explain how a single-time survey measures prevalence and why it struggles to establish temporality.

concepts.name: Randomized controlled trials
concepts.summary: Explain how randomization and a control group allow comparison of an intervention's effect.

concepts.name: Standardization of rates
concepts.summary: Apply age adjustment to compare rates between populations with different age structures.

misconceptions.text: The odds ratio is always interchangeable with the relative risk.
A high relative risk always means a large number of cases is attributable to the exposure.
Comparing crude rates between populations is always fair.

concepts.name: Selection bias mechanisms
concepts.summary: Analyse how participant selection, loss to follow-up and nonresponse distort associations.

concepts.name: Information bias and misclassification
concepts.summary: Distinguish differential from nondifferential misclassification and predict their effects on estimates.

concepts.name: Confounding identification
concepts.summary: Identify a confounder by its association with both exposure and outcome and its absence from the causal pathway.

concepts.name: Stratification and adjustment
concepts.summary: Control confounding through restriction, stratified analysis or multivariable regression.

concepts.name: Effect modification
concepts.summary: Distinguish effect modification from confounding by examining whether stratum-specific effects differ.

concepts.name: Confidence intervals and p-values
concepts.summary: Interpret confidence intervals around risk measures and separate statistical from clinical significance.

concepts.name: Outbreak investigation steps
concepts.summary: Apply the sequence of verifying the diagnosis, defining cases, finding cases, generating hypotheses and testing them.

concepts.name: Epidemic curves
concepts.summary: Interpret the shape of an epidemic curve to infer point-source versus propagated spread.

misconceptions.text: Any variable that changes the estimate when adjusted for is a confounder.
Misclassification always biases results toward the null.
A statistically significant result proves the association is causal and important.

concepts.name: Directed acyclic graphs
concepts.summary: Use DAGs to identify confounders, mediators and colliders and choose adjustment sets.

concepts.name: Causal inference frameworks
concepts.summary: Evaluate causal claims using the counterfactual framework and Bradford Hill considerations.

concepts.name: Collider and mediator bias
concepts.summary: Analyse how adjusting for mediators or colliders creates bias.

concepts.name: Survival and time-to-event analysis
concepts.summary: Interpret hazard ratios and censoring in time-to-event analyses.

concepts.name: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis
concepts.summary: Appraise pooled estimates, heterogeneity and publication bias in a body of evidence.

concepts.name: Screening and diagnostic accuracy
concepts.summary: Analyse how sensitivity, specificity and prevalence determine predictive values and screening biases like lead time.

concepts.name: Critical appraisal of studies
concepts.summary: Judge a study's validity by assessing design, bias, confounding, precision and generalizability.

misconceptions.text: Adjusting for more variables always gives a less biased estimate.
A test with high sensitivity and specificity has a high positive predictive value in any population.
Meta-analysis of many studies removes the biases in the individual studies.

concepts.name: Target trial emulation
concepts.summary: Design observational analyses that explicitly emulate a hypothetical randomized trial to avoid time-related biases.

concepts.name: Quasi-experimental methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate when natural experiments and instruments support causal estimates and which assumptions they require.

concepts.name: Mendelian randomization
concepts.summary: Appraise genetic-instrument analyses by testing relevance, independence and exclusion assumptions including pleiotropy.

concepts.name: Quantitative bias analysis
concepts.summary: Assess how strong unmeasured confounding or misclassification would have to be to explain a result.

concepts.name: Transmission modelling
concepts.summary: Evaluate compartmental models and reproduction numbers to project epidemics and compare interventions.

concepts.name: Surveillance system design
concepts.summary: Design a surveillance system that balances sensitivity, timeliness, representativeness and cost.

concepts.name: Study protocol design
concepts.summary: Create a protocol with a defensible design, power calculation, bias controls and pre-specified analysis plan.

concepts.name: Translating evidence into policy
concepts.summary: Weigh uncertain, conflicting evidence together with harms, equity and feasibility to recommend public health action.

misconceptions.text: An instrumental variable or Mendelian randomization analysis guarantees causal estimates regardless of assumptions.
The basic reproduction number is a fixed biological constant of a pathogen.
Sophisticated statistical modelling can fully compensate for a poorly designed study.
